scores.importance_reason: The gap aims to compare the prevalence of pregnancy weight gain among mothers whose infants experienced Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) versus those who had live births, using a case-population comparison design. While prior literature has identified maternal obesity as a risk factor for SUID, it does not directly address pregnancy weight gain specifically. This gap would refine current understanding by providing specific insights into the relationship between pregnancy weight gain and SUID.

The gap aims to compare the prevalence of maternal stressors during pregnancy between SUID (Sudden Unexpected Infant Death) cases and live births, using appropriate data sources within their coverage periods. This comparison could provide valuable insights into potential risk factors for SUID that are not yet well understood.

The gap addresses an important aspect of maternal health care utilization, which is known to influence pregnancy outcomes and infant health but has not been specifically studied in relation to Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID). This comparison could provide insights into whether inadequate prenatal care is a risk factor for SUID. The design aims to compare the prevalence of low prenatal healthcare utilization between SUID cases and a representative sample of live births, which can refine our understanding of potential modifiable risk factors.

This research gap aims to compare the prevalence of postpartum contraceptive use between mothers who experienced SUID (case series) and those in a representative sample from PRAMS (population reference). The design can establish an association but cannot determine causality or incidence rates due to differences in measurement timing and potential biases.

The gap addresses a critical aspect of understanding potential risk factors for Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) by examining maternal substance abuse, which is currently understudied compared to other known risk factors like smoking. This comparison between cases and a representative population sample can provide valuable insights into the prevalence and significance of this factor in SUID incidence.

The gap aims to quantify and compare the prevalence of infant sleep-sharing with adults between SUID cases and a general population sample of live-born infants, which would provide critical information on whether this behavior is more common in SUID cases than expected based on the broader population. This comparison could inform public health interventions by identifying behaviors that may be risk factors for SUID.

This research gap aims to compare the prevalence of previous preterm birth among mothers whose infants died due to sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) with that in the general population of new mothers. The design uses appropriate data sources for both case series (NCFRP) and population reference (PRAMS), allowing a valid comparison between these two groups.

The gap addresses a critical comparison of the prevalence of prenatal care issues among mothers of SUID cases versus the general population, which could provide important insights into risk factors for SUID. This comparison can refine current understanding by identifying specific prenatal factors that may influence SUID incidence rates.

The gap aims to compare the prevalence of hospital overnight stays among SUID cases and live births from PRAMS Phase 8. While this comparison can provide insights into whether infants who later experience SUID are more likely to have spent nights in the hospital after birth, it does not establish incidence rates or risks due to a lack of denominator source for SUID cases. It also cannot determine causality or control for confounders without additional data.

The gap addresses whether mothers of SUID cases are more likely to have experienced the death of a previous child compared to mothers of live births. This is an important research question because it could identify a previously unexplored risk factor for SUID and potentially inform preventive measures.

The proposed research would refine current understanding of the differences in medical complications between SUID cases and live births, which could provide important insights into potential risk factors for SUID.

The gap aims to compare the proportion of mothers with medical complications during pregnancy between those who experienced a Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) and the general population of new mothers. This comparison can refine current understanding by identifying potential risk factors associated with SUID, which could inform preventive measures and clinical practices.
The gap explores a novel association between maternal pre-pregnancy weight gain and SUID rates among prematurely-born infants, an area not fully addressed in existing literature.

The gap addresses a novel comparison between cesarean delivery and vaginal delivery in relation to the incidence of Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) using specific data sources that have not been used for this purpose before.

This study aims to determine whether the proportion of infants experiencing prenatal maternal stress differs between sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) cases and other causes of infant death using a case-case comparison design. It does not estimate incidence rates due to the lack of denominator data, but it can provide insights into potential risk factors by comparing proportions or odds.

The gap explores a specific comparison within infant deaths reviewed by NFR-CRS to identify whether hospitalizations for newborn complications are more common among SUID cases compared to non-SUID cases. This is important because it could provide insights into potential risk factors or underlying health conditions that may predispose infants to SUID, which has not been thoroughly investigated in existing literature.

The gap aims to determine if infants whose mothers did not receive adequate prenatal care are more likely to be SUID cases compared to other infant deaths within the NCFRP dataset. This study design can establish an association but cannot estimate incidence rates or risk ratios due to the lack of a denominator source that includes both live births and neonatal deaths for the same population during 2016-2019.

This gap aims to compare the proportion of SUID cases with inadequate postpartum healthcare access against non-SUID infant deaths, using case-case comparison designs. It addresses a critical aspect of understanding potential risk factors for SUID that are related to postnatal care and maternal health services.

This gap aims to identify distinct patterns in maternal factors between SUID cases and other causes of infant mortality using a case-case comparison, which is novel and would refine current understanding by providing insights into specific risk factors for SUID that are not observed in other types of infant deaths. This could help target interventions more effectively.

The gap addresses a potential difference in the use of postpartum contraception between SUID (Sudden Unexpected Infant Death) cases and other infant mortality cases. This comparison could provide insights into whether there are specific risk factors related to contraceptive use that might be associated with SUID, which is currently not well understood.

The gap aims to identify differences in maternal health conditions, insurance status, and healthcare utilization between SUID cases and other neonatal deaths within the same case series (NCFRP). This comparison could provide valuable insights into whether specific maternal factors are more prevalent among SUID cases compared to other neonatal deaths. Such information would help refine our understanding of risk factors for SUID and potentially inform preventive measures.

This gap aims to compare sleeping arrangements between SUID cases and non-SUID infant deaths using detailed data from the NCFRP dataset. It seeks to identify whether specific sleep environments are more common in SUID cases compared to other causes of infant death, which could provide insights into risk factors for SUID.

The gap addresses a novel aspect of pregnancy weight gain as a risk factor for SUID, which has not been extensively studied before. The case-case comparison design allows for valid comparisons within the same source (NCFRP), focusing on differences in proportions between SUID cases and other infant deaths without needing incidence rates or denominators from PRAMS.

The proposed study aims to compare the proportion of SUID cases with hospital overnight stays before discharge against other infant deaths using a case-case comparison design. This approach focuses on identifying differences in proportions among cases without requiring a denominator source for incidence or risk estimation.

The gap addresses an important research question about whether maternal health problems are differentially associated with SUID compared to other causes of infant death, which could inform targeted interventions and preventive measures.

The gap addresses a potential risk factor (previous hospitalizations for medical complications) that has not been specifically examined in relation to SUID cases, despite its relevance given the known associations with infant health and mortality.

The gap explores whether higher maternal prepregnancy body mass index (BMI) is associated with earlier postconceptional age at death in sudden unexpected infant death syndrome (SUID) cases. This study would refine current understanding by examining the relationship between maternal BMI and timing of SUID, which has not been thoroughly explored before.

The gap explores whether SUID cases with a history of previous child deaths have different sleep environment characteristics compared to those without such a history, using detailed information from the NCFRP dataset.

The case-only analysis compares maternal stressors between preterm and full-term SUID cases within the NCFRP dataset, but it does not provide incidence or risk ratios due to the absence of a population denominator. The design also cannot establish causation; only associations can be inferred.
This gap explores an important association between maternal intimate partner violence (IPV) and infant sleep surface sharing among SUID cases, which could inform preventive measures if confirmed.

This research gap aims to understand whether there are differences in patterns of prenatal care issues for SUID cases involving multiple gestation compared to singleton births, using only the case series data (NCFRP). It does not establish causality or incidence rates but focuses on comparing proportions or odds within the available case series. The closest prior work has excluded extremely and very preterm infants, leaving this specific comparison unexplored.

This gap aims to explore the variability in maternal gestational weight gain patterns among SUID (Sudden Unexpected Infant Death) cases across different pregnancy stages, using data from the National Fatality Review Case Reporting System (NCFRP). While this study will provide descriptive insights into how prenatal weight gain varies within SUID cases, it cannot establish causality or incidence rates due to its case-only design. The findings would be limited in their ability to draw causal conclusions but could offer valuable information on variations within the SUID population.

This research gap aims to understand whether there is a difference in the proportion of SUID (Sudden Unexpected Infant Death) cases that involve an overnight hospital stay compared to those that do not. This information could provide insights into potential risk factors or protective factors associated with hospital stays for infants at high risk of SUID.

The gap explores the relationship between maternal weight gain during pregnancy and pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI) categories within the context of sudden unexpected infant death syndrome (SUID). While prior literature suggests that maternal obesity increases SUID risk, this study aims to investigate how different levels of weight gain during pregnancy interact with pre-pregnancy BMI. This research would refine current understanding by providing more nuanced insights into how specific combinations of pre-pregnancy BMI and weight gain might influence SUID risk.

This gap explores the association between specific maternal health complications during pregnancy and their distribution among SUID cases, using a case-only approach. While it does not estimate incidence or odds ratios, it provides insights into whether there are differences in the proportion of SUID cases with various maternal health issues compared to those without such issues.

The gap aims to identify associations between postpartum depression and characteristics related to child neglect and abuse among SUID cases, using a case-only analysis. This can provide insights into potential risk factors for SUID that are associated with maternal mental health status.

The gap addresses a specific comparison within the SUID case series that has not been previously studied (hospital stay status and gestational age). It aims to understand if there is an association between these two variables among SUID cases, which could provide insights into potential risk factors or pathways for SUID. However, it does not establish incidence or causation due to its design limitations.

The gap explores whether the proportion of SUID cases with multiple gestation differs across postconceptional age, which could refine our understanding of risk factors and developmental patterns in SUID cases.

The gap addresses whether there is a significant difference in breastfeeding mode between SUID cases who were exclusively breastfed and those with mixed feeding methods. This comparison can refine understanding about potential risk factors for SUID but cannot establish incidence rates or causation due to the lack of denominator data.

The gap aims to understand whether there has been an increase in the proportion of SUID (Sudden Unexpected Infant Death) cases occurring within hospital overnight stays from 2016 to 2019. This information could be crucial for understanding changes in healthcare practices and their potential impact on infant mortality rates, particularly if hospitals are becoming more involved in preventing or managing conditions that lead to SUID. However, the study design can only compare proportions among cases and cannot estimate incidence or rates due to a lack of denominator data.

The gap aims to understand whether the proportion of SUID cases among infants with previous medical complications or disabilities has changed over time from 2012 to 2019. This is a novel question that could refine current understanding by identifying trends in the characteristics of SUID cases, which may inform targeted interventions and prevention strategies.

The gap aims to track trends in the proportion of SUID cases with substance/toxin exposure from 2004 to 2019 using ncfrp_v51 (case series). While this can provide descriptive information on changes over time within the case series, it cannot establish incidence or causal relationships due to lack of denominator data and inability to adjust for confounders effectively.

The gap aims to compare trends in hospital overnight stays among SUID cases with health care utilization trends reported by mothers in PRAMS, but it faces significant limitations in establishing incidence rates or causal relationships due to missing denominators and potential biases.

This gap focuses on the trend in documented pre-pregnancy health checks among SUID cases from 2012 to 2015, which has not been previously examined specifically for this outcome. The study design allows for comparison of trends within the case series but cannot estimate incidence or risk due to a lack of denominator data.

This gap aims to assess whether there has been a change over time in the proportion of SUID (Sudden Unexpected Infant Death) cases where mothers did not use birth control. The study design uses a case series and population reference, but lacks a denominator source necessary for estimating incidence rates or establishing causation.

This gap aims to compare the proportion of mothers with previous live births between SUID (Sudden Unexpected Infant Death) cases and live birth groups, using case series data from NCFRP and population reference data from PRAMS. It does not aim to estimate incidence rates due to missing denominator data for SUID cases but seeks to understand if there is a difference in the proportion of mothers with previous live births between these two groups.

This research gap addresses the comparison of maternal medical complications during pregnancy between SUID cases and live births using different data sources (NCFRP for case-level data on SUID cases and PRAMS for population reference surveys among mothers of live births). The study aims to fill a specific knowledge gap by comparing these proportions, acknowledging potential biases due to differences in measurement timing, wording, and reporting practices between the two sources. This comparison could refine current understanding about maternal health conditions as risk factors for SUID.

This gap addresses an important methodological issue in comparing data sources used for studying SUID (Sudden Unexpected Infant Death). The study aims to understand how pregnancy weight gain and postpartum smoking status are recorded differently between the NCFRP case series and PRAMS population reference, which can affect the validity of comparisons made using these datasets. This is crucial because discrepancies in recording methods could introduce bias into analyses comparing SUID cases with a general population sample.

The gap addresses how medical complications during pregnancy are recorded differently between the NCFRP case series and PRAMS population reference, which could introduce bias when comparing these sources. This is important for understanding potential discrepancies in exposure measurement that can affect case-population comparisons.

The gap addresses an important measurement issue in comparing case series and population reference data sources, specifically focusing on discrepancies in recording previous preterm births between NCFRP_v51 (case series) and PRAMS_P8_ARF (population reference). This is crucial for understanding potential biases in the comparison of detailed maternal history variables. The lack of prior work directly addressing this issue means that any findings would refine current understanding of how these data sources differ, which could impact the interpretation of existing studies and future research design.

This gap addresses the potential discrepancies in how prenatal care coordination issues are recorded in two different data sources (NCFRP_v51 and PRAMS_P7_ARF). Understanding these differences is crucial for accurate interpretation of case series versus population reference data, as it can affect the comparability and reliability of findings. This issue has not been addressed previously in the literature provided.

This gap focuses on comparing the recording of maternal stressors during pregnancy between NCFRP_v51 (case series) and PRAMS_P8_ARF (population reference). It aims to identify discrepancies in measurement methods and timing, which could affect how these variables are interpreted when used for case-population comparisons. The period overlap is limited but sufficient for a meaningful comparison within 2016-2019.

rule: Gaps rated below the minimum importance (or unrated) are filtered out. The rest are ranked by novelty x feasibility, highest first; a gap whose statement is at least the maximum similarity to one already shortlisted is skipped; selection stops at the shortlist size. (size 10, minimum importance 3, maximum similarity 0.85)
